question: What did Verity Payments say was the reason they left?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract the reasons Verity Payments gave for leaving or cancelling OrbitFlow, including any stated problems, competitor switches, budget or pricing issues, missing features, support concerns, and who gave each reason.
assumptions: 'Left' interpreted as churn, so restricted to Churn post-mortem calls.
Verity Payments matched exactly to the catalogue entry CALL-014.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
findings.context: Kwame Boateng said the connector gap was real but was not why Verity left; the real reason was that nobody in operations built anything and the platform was used as an engineering tool. — Customer contradicts Sarah's earlier framing of the connector gap as the cause; stated reason vs. real reason distinction.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Two years in, every single production workflow was built by Sarah's team.
findings.context: Verity's operations team never built workflows; every production workflow was built by Sarah's engineering team, so Verity paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. — Kwame's account of the underlying cause; Sarah confirms it.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: The difference is that we ended up writing a custom integration either way, and once you've accepted you're writing custom integrations, you start asking what the platform is actually giving you.
findings.context: Sarah Lindqvist said the connector for their settlement provider was missing, and that once they accepted writing custom integrations, they questioned what the platform was giving them for the price. — Sarah cites the February failure to build settlement reconciliation as the starting point of the decision.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations.
findings.context: Sarah Lindqvist said Verity left because they were maintaining custom integrations on a platform sold on not needing them, and the licence cost was justified by business-user autonomy that wasn't materialising. — Engineering-side reason for leaving.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
findings.context: Sarah's engineers wanted to build in-house, and Sarah eventually supported leaving after arguing against it for eighteen months. — Internal engineering preference contributed to the decision.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: It's partly a price decision, because at the margin we could justify one and not the other. But no, it's not primarily price.
findings.context: Kwame said the decision was not primarily about price; Workato was somewhat cheaper but not dramatically so. — Price was partly a factor but not the primary reason.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: Their connector for our core banking platform is genuinely better than yours. That one's just true.
findings.context: Verity chose Workato over OrbitFlow because Workato's core banking connector was better and its engineering-facing story (recipes as code, CI) was stronger. — Competitor switch reasons given by Sarah.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.context: Verity felt treated as a small account; support was inconsistent, though Sarah said support was not why they left. — Secondary grievance that contributed to the general feeling of being a small account.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: That's when it was over, if you want the specific moment.
findings.context: Verity's April connector problem during the Workato PoC was resolved by Workato with an unbilled solutions architect building a custom connector, which Sarah said was the moment the decision ended. — OrbitFlow had only offered a template search and an email saying none existed.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: I think we were the wrong customer for the product, or the product was sold to us for the wrong reason.
findings.context: Kwame said the product and sales process were the real issue: Verity was sold on enthusiasm rather than capability, and OrbitFlow did not offer the paid professional services that would have made the team self-sufficient. — Kwame's view on the wrong-customer/wrong-reason sale, from his own experience.

draft.answer: Verity's two speakers gave different accounts of why they left. Kwame Boateng said the connector gap was only what they pointed at, and the real cause was that operations never built workflows and the platform was used as an engineering tool [C1][C2]. Sarah Lindqvist said they were maintaining custom integrations on a platform sold on not needing them, so the cost was hard to justify [C3]. They moved to Workato, with a better core banking connector and a PoC rescue as the final moment, and price was not the primary factor [C4][C5].

claims.text: Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations) said the connector gap was real but was not why Verity left; it was 'the thing we pointed at'.

Kwame said the underlying cause was that Verity's operations team never built workflows: every production workflow was built by Sarah's engineering team, so Verity paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. He also said Verity was the wrong customer, or was sold the product for the wrong reason (sold on enthusiasm rather than capability, with no paid professional services offered).

Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager) said the missing settlement-provider connector led them to write custom integrations, and then to question what the platform gave them for the price. She said they left because they maintained custom integrations on a platform whose selling point was not needing them, and the licence cost was justified by business-user autonomy that wasn't materialising. Her engineers also wanted to build in-house, and after eighteen months of arguing against it she ran out of arguments.

Verity chose Workato: Sarah said its core banking connector is genuinely better and its engineering-facing story (recipes as code, CI) is stronger. The decisive moment was the April PoC, when Workato had an unbilled solutions architect build a custom connector while OrbitFlow offered only a template search and an email saying none existed.

Kwame said the decision was partly price, since Workato was somewhat cheaper, but not primarily price. Sarah said inconsistent support contributed to Verity feeling like a small account, but was not why they left.

conflicts.description: Kwame said the connector gap was not the real reason and that the root cause was operations never building workflows. Sarah framed the connector gap and custom integration maintenance as the starting point and reason for the decision.

assumptions: 'Left' interpreted as churn, restricted to the Churn post-mortem call CALL-014 with Verity Payments.
